notes.trap: `coalesce(...)` only skips SQL NULL. A floating-point NaN counts as a real value, so it is returned as is. Use `nanvl(...)` to replace NaN.
A NULL condition is not an error and is not propagated as NULL. It is treated as not true, so the third argument (the else branch) is returned.
`nanvl(...)` replaces only NaN, not NULL. A NULL first argument gives NULL rather than the fallback, unlike `nvl(...)` or `coalesce(...)`.
The equality test uses implicit type coercion, so a string and a number can compare equal. With ANSI off, the string is cast to the numeric type and the result becomes NULL.

`nvl(...)` is rewritten to `coalesce(...)`, so both arguments are coerced to a common type. Mixing a number with a string literal silently makes the result a STRING, even when the first value is used.
`nvl2(...)` tests only whether expr1 is NULL. It never returns expr1, and a non-NULL falsy value such as 0 or false still selects expr2.
In the simple form CASE x WHEN NULL, the match is tested with =, so it never matches, even when x is NULL. Use the searched form CASE WHEN x IS NULL instead.
notes.example_sql: SELECT CASE CAST(NULL AS INT) WHEN NULL THEN 'matched' ELSE 'no match' END
